column3: Exact parallel: entering Hell's gates eternally is called the wretched abode of the arrogant.
The immediately preceding verse brings disbelievers in groups to Hell and opens its gates before this command.
It joins arrogant rejection of God's signs to humiliating punishment at death, supplying the moral cause.
Exact parallel in wording and judgment: enter Hell's gates eternally, the wretched abode of the arrogant.
Its warning that idolaters lose themselves and their families on Resurrection Day frames the loss realized in 39:72.
The instruction on protecting vulnerable heirs and speaking rightly does not illuminate the judgment scene.
Hell is described as a wretched resting place, a close formulaic counterpart without gates or arrogance.
An opened gate leads to severe punishment and despair, but its setting is not the final Hell abode.
The great sign shown to Pharaoh precedes a paradigmatic case of arrogant rejection, only indirectly related.
It names Hell as the abode of the arrogant and depicts their humiliation on the Day of Resurrection.
The next verse deliberately contrasts the condemned group's Hell-gate entry with the righteous entering Paradise eternally.
Mutual sinful alliance culminates in Fire as an eternal abode, closely matching permanent punitive dwelling.
Those entering punishment call it a wretched place of settlement, echoing the verdict on the abode.
It identifies the truthful and those who affirm truth as the God-fearing, a local contrast to the condemned.
Moses' declaration of his mission to Pharaoh has no direct link to Hell, entry, or eternal punishment.
It uses multiple gates and entry language, but only for Jacob's practical travel instruction.
The people's refusal to enter a land because of tyrants only shares the vocabulary of entering.
It explicitly asks whether Hell is not an abode for disbelievers who forge lies and reject truth.
The eternal good dwelling of Paradise provides a clear evaluative contrast to Hell's wretched abode.
The praise of Paradise's inheritors is a nearby positive outcome, but lacks the focus verse's punitive terms.
Believers enter gardens eternally; this is the positive counterpart to the permanent entry in 39:72.
Associating partners with God leads to Fire as a wretched abode for wrongdoers, closely paralleling the judgment.
Its question names Hell as the abode for those who lie about God and reject truth, setting up the local contrast.
It warns against status-seeking treachery between communities, touching arrogance only indirectly.
Proud persistence in sin is answered with Hell as a wretched resting place, matching cause and destination.
Crossing a gate in trust is a positive, historical use of entry imagery rather than an afterlife parallel.
The opened gates of heaven concern the flood, sharing only the boundary imagery.
The righteous are welcomed by angels and told to enter Paradise, a concise positive inverse of 39:72.
The nearby warning of fire enclosing its inhabitants develops the punishment announced in the focus passage.
Marriage prohibitions do not clarify Hell, eternal residence, or arrogance.
The command to enter wholly into submission is conceptually opposed to defiant rejection but otherwise distant.
Those arrogant toward God's signs are denied heavenly gates and Paradise, directly joining arrogance and barred entry.
It distinguishes human mortality from everlasting life, only loosely related to eternal residence after judgment.
Secret sinful defiance ends in Hell, called a wretched destination, though it lacks the focus wording.
The nearby promise of lofty Paradise dwellings contrasts with Hell but does not specify entry or arrogance.
Entry into divine mercy for the righteous is a broad positive contrast to entry into Hell.
The command to enter Paradise joyfully supplies a direct positive inverse to the command in 39:72.
It condemns taking protectors besides God and insists on pure religion, a local cause of the condemned outcome.
The statement that all things are recorded offers no specific connection to the focus judgment.
A condemned person calls his companion wretched in the hereafter, echoing the adverse final companionship.
Creation and exclusive divine lordship do not directly clarify the Hell-entry judgment.
Pharaoh's arrogant denial of return to God identifies the disposition reversed by the final judgment.
God commands successive communities to enter the Fire, where they gather and curse one another.
Even an opened heavenly gate would not persuade persistent deniers, a distant gate-and-rejection parallel.
Qarun, Pharaoh, and Haman arrogantly reject clear signs yet cannot escape God's reckoning.
Believers receive eternal pleasant dwellings in gardens, a substantial positive contrast to Hell's abode.
The claim of bewitched sight concerns denial of signs but not the focus verse's final punishment.
Arrogance and evil plotting recoil on their practitioners, supporting the reversal underlying the judgment.
Refusing the command to bow exemplifies defiant pride, though the verse does not state its punishment.
Closed doors and a dwelling appear in Joseph's moral trial, but not as eschatological entry or punishment.
Iblis refuses and acts arrogantly, becoming a disbeliever: the foundational pattern of the focus verdict.
House-entry etiquette and permission are unrelated to the punitive gates of Hell.
The God-fearing enter lasting gardens, an afterlife counterpart opposite to eternal residence in Hell.
The arrogant explicitly reject the faith affirmed by the weak, directly characterizing the condemned disposition.
Doubt and denial of the assured Hour explain the disbelief that culminates in final punishment.
The command to enter the holy land is a historical and positive use of entry language.
The wretched person enters the greatest Fire, a close but compressed punishment counterpart.
The question about alleged partners exposes shirk immediately before the parallel command to enter Hell's gates.
Secure entry into the Sacred Mosque is a positive fulfillment scene, sharing only entry imagery.
Entry into eternal gardens presents a sustained positive contrast to the condemned eternal abode.
The only path for the rejecting is Hell, where they remain forever, directly matching the permanence of 39:72.
Inexhaustible provision in Paradise is only a distant contrast to everlasting punitive dwelling.
They respond arrogantly when told that there is no god but God, linking arrogance to core disbelief.
The deceiver and follower end together in Fire, remaining there eternally as the recompense of wrongdoers.
Paradise gates are opened for the righteous, a deliberate positive contrast to Hell's gates.
Wealth and children cannot avert God's judgment; their possessors are companions of Fire, remaining forever.
Disbelievers are defeated, gathered to Hell, and assigned a wretched resting place.
Near victory and divine help do not illuminate final punishment or arrogance.
It specifies enduring residence in Hell under God's will, clarifying the focus verse's permanence.
Iblis and his followers are destined to fill Hell, connecting arrogant rebellion with that final destination.
The punishment is multiplied and the offender remains in it humiliated, closely matching permanent degradation.
Those who follow Iblis receive Hell as a full recompense, a related final-destination warning.
Turning away and acting arrogantly concisely names the posture opposed by the focus verse.
The guilty remain eternally in the punishment of Hell, directly paralleling the permanent abode.
Guidance on managing dependents' property has no meaningful connection to the focus judgment.
God's final dismissal, "remain in it," conveys irreversible exclusion in the Hell judgment scene.
The people of the Heights tell recognizable arrogant people that their amassed status did not benefit them.
Disbelievers and polytheists remain eternally in Hellfire and are called the worst creatures.
The wealthy man boasts of greater wealth and company, a concrete portrayal of self-exalting status.
Those who disbelieve and deny signs are companions of Fire, remaining there eternally in a wretched end.
Entering the gate prostrate and seeking forgiveness is a positive humility contrast to arrogance.
Hypocrites and disbelievers are promised Hellfire, remaining there eternally in lasting punishment.
The companion challenges the wealthy man's disbelief and recalls his humble created origin, correcting pride.
Those too arrogant to worship God will enter Hell humiliated, directly joining arrogance, entry, and abasement.
Whether they endure or seek pardon, Fire remains their abode, underscoring the settled punitive residence.
Whoever disobeys God and His messenger has Hellfire, remaining there forever.
It warns those who attribute a child to God, a form of disbelief only indirectly tied to the focus outcome.
Truthful believers are rewarded with gardens beneath which rivers flow, remaining there eternally, the positive inverse.
Travel fatigue after passing a meeting point has no connection to the judgment vocabulary or theme.
The cursed remain in punishment without relief or reprieve, strongly clarifying irreversible permanence.
Opposing God and His messenger earns Hellfire, remaining there eternally, called the great disgrace.
Abraham's immediate submission provides a broad humility contrast to refusal and arrogance.
The corrupt are gathered together and placed in Hell as the losers, a related judgment outcome.
Deniers evade clear signs by demanding their ancestors be brought back, showing resurrection denial.
Raised couches in Paradise do not meaningfully clarify Hell, arrogance, or the judgment.
Those whose scales are light lose themselves and remain eternally in Hell.
Inheritance allocations have no relevant semantic or thematic connection.
The human question to the earth during the quake does not explain the focus verse's condemnation.
Selective rejection of revelation is related disbelief but has no direct Hell, permanence, or arrogance link.
Mockers call believers astray, without an explicit connection to the final Hell-entry judgment.
Those who deny God's signs and act arrogantly are companions of the Fire, remaining there eternally.
The arrogant deniers receive Hell as bed and covering, a vivid image of inescapable punitive residence.
Those who earn evil become companions of the Fire, remaining there eternally after their faces are darkened.
The wretched are in the Fire, where they cry out, directly naming the condemned group whose duration 11:107 specifies.
Those who disbelieve in the Hereafter are companions of the Fire, remaining there eternally.
It names Hell as the destination and a wretched dwelling for those who exchange God's favor for disbelief.
Hell is the promised destination for all of Iblis's followers, supplying the broader judgment setting.
Hell has seven gates, a uniquely direct parallel to the gates commanded open in the focus verse.
Those who choose the fleeting world may be assigned Hell, entering it condemned and banished.
For wrongdoers, Fire encloses them and is prepared as an evil resting place.
Whoever comes to God as a criminal has Hell, where one neither dies nor lives.
Whenever they try to leave the Fire in anguish, they are returned to it, stressing irreversible confinement.
The servants of the Merciful seek protection from Hell's punishment because it is an inescapable affliction.
Hell is explicitly called an evil settlement and dwelling, closely echoing the focus verdict on its abode.
Hell surrounds the disbelievers, emphasizing the encompassing final punishment.
The wicked have Fire as their refuge; every attempted exit returns them to it.
Disbelievers remain in Hell, where death and the punishment's severity are not lightened.
The decree of punishment against disbelievers is fulfilled: they are companions of the Fire.
Pharaoh's people are exposed to Fire and, at the Hour, are commanded into the severest punishment.
Those who forgot the meeting with God are abandoned to Fire, their refuge, with no helpers.
Disbelievers take their enjoyment while the Fire is their final lodging, contrasting worldly pride with outcome.
The command to cast every stubborn, ungrateful opponent into Hell portrays the judicial entry into punishment.
For hypocrites and disbelievers, Fire is the only refuge and an evil destination.
The mighty, severe angels guarding Hell reinforce the controlled punitive realm entered in 39:72.
Those who disbelieve have the punishment of Hell, described as an evil destination.
The divine command to cast the condemned into Hell directly parallels the focus verse's command of entry.
God declares that He will drive the rejecter into Saqar, a direct threat of Hellfire.
Hell lies in ambush as the appointed place of return for transgressors.
Transgressors remain in Hell for ages, strengthening the focus verse's enduring-residence theme.
The wicked will enter the blazing Fire, a concise direct counterpart to the command in 39:72.
